title: Deterministic polynomial-time construction of a prime of a given bit length
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm and constants \(C,c>0\) which, on input \(1^{n}\) for every \(n\ge 2\), output a prime p with \(2^{n- 1}\le p<2^{n}\) in at most \(Cn^{c}\) bit operations?
definitions: Use uniform classical deterministic Turing computation, with no advice or oracle. Integers and rational numerators and denominators are encoded in binary; L denotes the total input bit length. A polynomial bound has constants independent of the input. The unary input parameter requests an n-bit output. A prime is an integer greater than one with no positive divisors other than one and itself. Correctness and the bound must hold for every \(n\ge 2\); neither randomization, an oracle, a prime table supplied as advice, nor an unproved number-theoretic hypothesis is allowed.

context_blocks.text: Primality testing and finding a prime are different algorithmic tasks. A quickly checkable certificate for a candidate does not by itself identify a candidate in a prescribed bit-length interval.

Random sampling efficiently finds primes, while deterministic generation is a classical explicit-construction problem tied to derandomization and time-bounded information. The source uses the sequence of primes produced by deterministic search to explain that connection. Pseudodeterministic randomized generation also leaves this all-input deterministic target unresolved.
